nameStory: This graceful shrub is named after Carl Peter Thunberg, an 18th-century Swedish botanist who was one of the first Europeans to study Japanese plants extensively. Thunberg spent years in Japan during the 1770s, when the country was largely closed to foreigners, and he discovered many Asian plants that were completely unknown to Western science at the time.
description: Thunberg's lespedeza is an elegant deciduous shrub that creates cascading fountains of pink-purple flowers in late summer. This Asian native typically grows 3-6 feet tall with long, arching branches that give it a graceful, weeping appearance. Like other members of the legume family, it has the characteristic three-leaflet leaves and pea-like flowers, making it both beautiful and beneficial for soil health.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to rose-purple pea-like flowers cluster densely along the drooping branch tips in late summer, creating spectacular cascading displays that feel papery to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Distinctive arching, fountain-like form with long flexible branches that curve downward and often touch the ground, creating an almost weeping willow effect

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three oval leaflets per leaf (typical of legumes), each about an inch long, with a smooth texture and blue-green color that turns yellow in fall

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flat, oval pods about a quarter-inch long that turn brown and feel papery when ripe, often persisting into winter

habitat: In New England, Thunberg's lespedeza is primarily found as an ornamental escape or naturalized plant in disturbed areas, roadsides, and woodland edges. It prefers well-drained soils and full to partial sun, often establishing itself near old gardens or abandoned homesteads where it was originally planted.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in spring, appearing as small clusters of three leaflets on bare woody stems. The shrub leafs out much later than most native plants.
seasonality.summer: The spectacular flowering display begins in mid to late summer, with pink-purple blooms covering the gracefully arching branches through August and September.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, while the small brown seed pods develop and often persist on the branches after leaf fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare arching branches create an elegant winter silhouette, often with small brown seed pods still clinging to the twigs.

funFact: This shrub is essentially a natural soil factory - like all legumes, it has special bacteria living in nodules on its roots that capture nitrogen from the air and convert it into fertilizer, actually improving the soil around it as it grows!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with shrub lespedeza (Lespedeza bicolor), but Thunberg's has a much more pronounced weeping, fountain-like growth habit with longer arching branches, while shrub lespedeza grows more upright and bushy.
contextualKnowledge: Though beautiful, this Asian native can be somewhat aggressive in spreading and may outcompete native plants in some areas. Many gardeners love it for late-season color, but it's worth considering native alternatives like wild bergamot or New England asters for supporting local ecosystems.
compareHints: Among the lespedezas, Thunberg's is unique for its dramatic weeping form - most other bush clovers in New England grow upright or spreading but not with these long, graceful drooping branches. The late summer flowering time and fountain-like shape make it quite distinctive from its more modest native cousins like round-headed bush clover.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Round-headed bush clover stands out from its Lespedeza relatives by its distinctly round, compact flower heads - most other bush clovers have loose, elongated flower clusters or flowers scattered along the stems.
Among New England's bush clovers, hairy lespedeza stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture covering the entire plant.
Among its bush clover relatives, violet bush clover stands out with its smooth (not hairy) stems and leaves, and its loose flower arrangement rather than dense round clusters.
Among New England's bush clovers, Chinese bushclover stands out for its silvery, densely hairy appearance and aggressive colonial growth habit.
Among New England's bush clovers, slender bush clover stands out for its delicate, wispy appearance with thin stems and small flower clusters.

Among its bush-clover relatives, tall bush-clover stands out with its reliably erect stems - round-headed bush clover has similar upright growth but denser, more rounded flower clusters, while violet bush clover and trailing lespedeza have more sprawling or leaning growth habits.
Among the many Lespedeza species, shrub lespedeza is unique in New England for its tall, shrubby growth habit - most other bush clovers in our region are low-growing or trailing plants.
Unlike its upright relatives like round-headed bush clover or hairy lespedeza that can reach several feet tall, trailing lespedeza never gets off the ground.
Among its bush clover relatives, narrow-leaved bush clover stands out for its distinctly slender leaflets and preference for wet soils.
Among the bush clovers in New England, violet bush clover stands out for its distinctly purple-violet flowers - most of its relatives have white, cream, or very pale pink blooms.
While most of its lespedeza relatives like round-headed bush clover and violet bush clover grow upright in bushy clumps, creeping lespedeza is the ground-hugger of the family.
Downy lespedeza stands out from other bush clovers in New England primarily by its extremely fuzzy, silvery appearance.
